overview: Orthodontists are dental specialists who straighten teeth and correct jaw problems. They examine patients, study X-rays, scans and models of the teeth, then design and adjust braces, aligners and retainers over months or years. O*NET rates knowledge of medicine and dentistry at 4.95 out of 5 for this job, and monitoring and critical thinking at 4. Becoming one takes dental school plus a 2 to 3 year orthodontics residency. The BLS May 2025 median is $289,140, in a small field of 6,210 jobs. Most run or join private practices and lead a team of assistants.
pay: Orthodontists earn a median of $289,140, and the top 10% earn $416,000 or more. Connecticut has the highest state median at $478,680, 66% above the national figure, followed by Colorado. BLS publishes state data for only 19 states, and Washington has the most jobs among them, 290.

faq.a: The BLS May 2025 median is $289,140 a year. The middle half earn between $146,580 and $342,300, and practice owners are usually at the top. Connecticut, Colorado ($416,000) and Maryland ($361,030) have the highest state medians among states with published data.

faq.q: How long does it take to become an orthodontist?
faq.a: It usually takes 4 years of college, 4 years of dental school and a residency in orthodontics of 2 to 3 years. O*NET places the job in Job Zone 5. After residency, most orthodontists take board exams and a state specialty license before practicing.

faq.q: What is a typical day for an orthodontist?
faq.a: Most days are full of short patient visits to check progress and adjust braces or aligners, plus new patient exams. In O*NET data the job ranks above 99% of U.S. jobs for leading others and above 96% for working with people, since you direct a busy clinic team.

O*NET rates active listening, speaking, critical thinking and monitoring at 4 out of 5 for this job. Knowledge of customer service is rated 4.25, because most patients are children and teens with their parents. Fine hand skills and attention to detail are essential.
